To cure myself of wanting Cuban songs, I wrote a Cuban song about the need For people to suppress their fantasies, Especially unhealthy ones. The song Began by making reference to the sea, Because the sea is like a need so great And deep it never can be swallowed. Then The song explores some common myths About the Cuban people and their folklore: The story of a little Carib boy Mistakenly abandoned to the sea; The legend of a bird who wanted song So desperately he gave up flight; a queen Whose strength was greater than a rival king’s. The song is ending now, because I cannot bear to hear it any longer. I call this song of needful love my voice.

Keywords: Cuban, For, Especially

outputs.L1: To cure myself of longing for Cuban songs, I composed one—a song about the necessity of suppressing our fantasies, especially those unwholesome ones we harbor. The song opened with an invocation of the sea, for the sea embodies a need so vast, so fathomless, it can never be sated. From there, the song ventured into the enduring myths of the Cuban people, their folklore woven through time: the tale of a young Carib boy, cast adrift upon the waves by cruel mistake; the legend of a bird whose yearning for song was so profound that it forsook flight altogether; and a queen whose fortitude eclipsed that of a rival king. The song turned then toward questions of morality, before circling back once more to the sea—its depths, the countless creatures sustained by its bounty, and the strange beauty inherent in longing itself. Now the song draws to its close, for I can no longer bear its sound. This song of aching love, I call my voice.

# On Writing a Cuban Song

I wrote a Cuban song to cure myself of wanting Cuban songs—a strange remedy, perhaps, but one born of necessity. There is a particular danger in unchecked longing, in allowing fantasy to calcify into something unhealthy, something that feeds on itself without ever reaching satisfaction. So I turned to the only cure I knew: to write the very thing I craved, to exhaust the desire by giving it form, by making it mine rather than letting it remain an ache without shape.

The song begins, as so much begins, with the sea. I reached for an extended metaphor, letting the ocean become need itself—vast, dark, depthless. The sea does not fill; it does not satisfy. It swallows and swallows and is never full, never quiet, never done asking for more. This is the nature of true need, I wrote: bottomless, insatiable, older than memory, older than any single hunger. The waves do not crash to conclusion; they simply continue, an endless rhythm of wanting.

From this opening, I turned to the old stories, the folklore that Cuba has carried across centuries like driftwood on that same insatiable sea. There is the Carib boy, abandoned to the water by those who should have protected him, left to face the depths alone—a figure of abandonment that already speaks to something essential in the human experience of need. There is the bird who traded flight for song, who gave up the sky itself so that beauty might exist in sound rather than in soaring—a sacrifice that suggests something is always given up so something else might be gained. And there is the queen, powerful and unyielding, who faced down a rival king and did not break, whose strength became its own kind of music. These are not simply old tales; I wove them through my verses because they carry the weight of a people's understanding about sacrifice, endurance, and the cost of survival.

The song does not stay comfortable in myth alone. It turns, as these things must, toward questions of morality—toward what we owe each other, what we take, what we lose in the taking. But I could not leave it there in that difficult terrain. The song circles back to the sea, because that is where the truth lives most clearly. There is beauty in need itself, I discovered as I wrote—not despite the hunger, but within it. The depth of the sea, after all, is what nourishes so many creatures; its very insatiability is what makes it a source of life. Need is not simply emptiness. It is also abundance, if you know how to look at it, if you are willing to see the depths not as a void but as a wellspring.

And yet, in the end, I could not bear to keep listening to what I had made. The song, once given voice, revealed too much—showed too clearly the shape of my own wanting, my own bottomless sea. So I stopped it. I ended the song before it could end itself, before it could swallow me the way the sea swallows everything that enters it.

What I created, I now understand, was needful love given voice—my own voice, discovered through metaphor and myth, through the old stories and the new ache. I wrote a Cuban song to cure myself of wanting Cuban songs, and in doing so, I found that the cure and the disease were, perhaps, always the same thing: the simple, unrelenting truth of desire, given words because it could not be denied.
outputs.L4:
# The Cure I Wrote in Salt

I sat by the window where the Straits go dark blue to black
and told myself: make a song, small enough to hold,
a thing you can sing until the wanting goes quiet.
This is how sickness works — you name it, you rock it,
you drown it in verses the way the old women
drowned their grief in rum and prayer.

So I began with water, because water is patient,
because water forgets nothing and holds everything anyway.
I wrote: *the sea does not choose what it keeps.*
I wrote it again, changed one word, called it progress.

## I. The Boy Who Went Under

They tell it different on every coast, but the bones agree:
a Carib boy swam out past where the reef breaks color,
chasing something bright he thought was a fish,
and the current took the wanting and gave back nothing,
not even a body to grieve over properly.
His mother still stands on the rock at Baracoa,
though no one has seen her in four hundred years —
only the shape the wind makes when it curves around absence.

I used him in the second verse. I made him a metaphor
for the thing I couldn't have, dressed grief up
as folklore so it would sit still long enough to rhyme.
*Some hungers,* I wrote, *are only the sea remembering it swallowed something once.*
I thought this was wisdom. I thought naming was the same as healing.

## II. The Bird Who Traded Wings

There is an old story, the kind grandmothers tell
to quiet children who want too much too loudly:
a bird once flew higher than any bird should,
and God, or something like God, said *choose* —
the sky or the song, you cannot keep both hungers.
The bird chose singing. It has walked the earth since,
wingless, astonishing, unbearable to hear
because every note carries the memory of altitude
it will never touch again.

I put the bird in the bridge of my song
because I too was trying to trade one hunger for another —
give up the wanting-of-you for the singing-about-wanting-you,
as if that were not the same appetite
wearing a different, more presentable coat.
As if grounding the wings made the sky less missed.

## III. The Queen Who Ruled the Deep

And there was a queen — there is always a queen
in the stories we tell to explain why desire drowns us —
who ruled the water the way some women rule a room:
without raising her voice, without needing to.
Men went under for her willingly. It wasn't cruelty.
It was gravity. It was the shape water takes
around anything with enough weight to matter.

I made her the chorus. I made her the reason
the boy went swimming, the reason the bird
gave up the sky for something closer to a voice.
I thought if I could give my wanting a name and a crown
I could bow to it once, formally, and be done.

## IV. What the Song Became

But songs are not cages. I built this one
to hold the wanting still, and instead it grew teeth.
Every time I sang it the sea got louder,
the boy stayed under longer, the bird's missing wings
ached in places I didn't know a metaphor could reach,
and the queen — the queen simply watched,
because queens know that need dressed as art
is still need, is still the old current
pulling you toward the bright thing you can't have,
now with better cadence, now with a bridge that modulates
directly into the same four notes of longing.

I could not sing it anymore. Not because I'd healed
but because I'd finally heard what I'd been making:
not a cure, not even a container,
but a mirror shaped like music,
in which the wanting looked back at me
and I understood, too late for it to comfort,
that this — the writing, the naming, the folkloric hiding —
was never separate from the love itself.
The song did not describe the need.
The song *was* the need, dressed for company,
and I was not its author so much as its latest verse,
another voice added to the boy's, the bird's, the queen's,
singing the same drowning
in the only key I have ever known how to survive in.

The sea does not choose what it keeps.
Neither, it turns out, do I.
outputs.L5:
# Cuban Culture and Its Enduring Appeal

Cuban culture holds a special place in the hearts of many who encounter it, whether through music, food, or history. For those who have experienced the rhythmic pulse of Havana's streets, the connection often becomes lifelong. The island nation offers a unique blend of Spanish, African, and Caribbean influences that have combined to create something truly distinctive.

For travelers seeking an authentic experience, Cuba provides a glimpse into a world that feels both timeless and evolving. Classic cars still cruise the streets alongside newer vehicles, and colonial architecture stands as a testament to centuries of history. Especially in cities like Trinidad and Havana, visitors can witness this fascinating juxtaposition of past and present.

Cuban music deserves particular attention, having influenced genres worldwide. Especially notable is how son, salsa, and rumba emerged from this small island to captivate global audiences. Musicians like Buena Vista Social Club brought international recognition to traditional Cuban sounds, introducing new generations to rhythms that had been perfected over decades.

The cuisine, too, tells a story of resourcefulness and flavor. For many, dishes like ropa vieja, moros y cristianos, and fresh seafood represent comfort food with deep cultural roots. Especially in family-run paladares, visitors can taste recipes passed down through generations, each meal offering insight into Cuban resilience and creativity despite economic challenges.

Beyond the tourist experience, Cuban people themselves often leave the deepest impression. Their warmth, resilience, and joy in the face of hardship speak to a national character forged by decades of complex political and economic circumstances. For anyone willing to look beyond surface-level observations, Cuba offers profound lessons about community, adaptation, and the human spirit's capacity to find beauty even in difficult circumstances.

Whether through dance, art, literature, or simple daily interactions, Cuban culture continues to captivate and inspire people around the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in blank verse about writing a song to cure yourself of a longing, using Cuban folklore and the sea as central images.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cantar para Curarme**

I sit where Yemayá keeps her blue house,
the tide-line stitched with foam like altar lace,
and try to build a song to bury this—
this longing that has followed me like smoke
from Havana's rooftops to a colder shore.
The old ones say the sea remembers names
we have forgotten, holds them in her mouth
like stones worn smooth by centuries of no.
So I begin with what my grandmother
once hummed while shelling black beans on the porch,
a tune half prayer, half warning, all Yoruba
bent through Spanish till it sounded like
a secret only water understood.

I write a verse the way you'd cast a shell,
not knowing yet which answer it will show—
heads-up for yes, the dark side down for wait.
I sing the name I will not say by name,
folding it into rhythm like a leaf
folded around an offering of rum.
The waves keep time, indifferent and exact,
the way the orishas are indifferent,
loving us best when we don't ask for love.

Ochún would tell me: sweeten it with honey,
make longing dance until it's tired enough
to sleep. But I am calling on the sea,
not the river—Yemayá is patience,
seventeen years of waiting in one wave.
I write another line, and try to mean
the letting go instead of holding on.
The ceiba by the shoreline drops no leaves;
its roots go down through everyone I've lost.
I tie my longing to its lowest branch
the way the santeros tie their ribbons,
red and white, asking to be forgiven
for wanting what the ocean cannot give.

By the last verse, the song has turned to salt—
not sweet, not bitter, just the taste of having
carried something far enough to drop it.
I do not know if I am cured. I know
the tide came in and took the words I wrote
and did not bring them back. That has to count
as mercy, or as close as I will get,
here at the edge where every Cuban song
was born already halfway out to sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective, meta poem about creating a "Cuban song" that explores need, myth, and morality, ending with a personal revelation about voice.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Being Asked to Write a Cuban Song

I sit down to write you Cuba
and find I am writing hunger instead—
not the song itself but the wanting of it,
the space where a trumpet should enter
and doesn't, or enters wrong,
borrowed from a record I half-remember,
a grandmother's kitchen that isn't mine.

What do I know of son, of clave,
except that it counts itself
in threes and twos like a heart
deciding which rhythm to trust?
I could give you palm trees.
I could give you rum-sweet metaphors,
a woman named Esperanza dancing
in a doorway that smells of salt.
I could make the myth so easily—
island as body, body as song,
suffering rendered lyrical,
poverty made to shimmer
like something worth wanting.

This is the old temptation:
to borrow grief for its music,
to wear a place like a scarf
because the color moves me.

But whose need is this song answering?
Not Cuba's. Cuba does not need
another elegy from outside,
another cigar-smoke reverie.
This need is mine—
to prove I can hold a country
in four stanzas, make it sing
on command, make myth
do the labor memory should.

So let me stop pretending
this is Cuba's song at all.
Let me call it what it is:
a poem about wanting to write
something I have no right to own,
about the morality of borrowed music,
about how easily longing
becomes appropriation
when it forgets to ask permission.

I came here to make an island sing.
Instead I found my own voice,
thin and uncertain,
asking the only honest question:
not *what does Cuba sound like*
but *what am I, that I would take it—*

and the answer arrives quietly,
underneath the false rhythm I started with:
I am someone still learning
that some songs are not mine to write,
only mine to listen to,
standing at the door,
hands empty,
finally quiet enough to hear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a poem where the speaker tries to purge a desire by composing a fictional song, weaving in invented legends and ending on an emotional confession?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Song I Made to Forget You

I invented a legend to bury this wanting—
told myself a river-girl loved a stone so long
she turned to water just to hold him,
and every spring the thaw is her forgiveness.
I made that up. There is no river-girl.
There is only me, at 2 a.m., turning you
into myth because the truth was too small
to hold this much grief.

I sang of a king who traded his crown
for one more hour with a shadow that spoke
like someone he'd lost—
and how the shadow always left at dawn,
as shadows do, as you did,
though you were never mine to lose,
not really, not the way the songs demand.

I built a whole mythology:
the sailor who heard his dead wife's voice
in every conch shell on the shore,
the god who wept so hard he made the sea,
the twin moons that orbit each other
forever almost touching—
I thought if I dressed this ache in old language,
gave it robes and thrones and drowned kingdoms,
I could set it down somewhere outside my chest,
let it live in the story instead of in me.

But here's the confession beneath the invention:
I don't want the myth. I want you
on a Tuesday, in bad light,
saying my name like it's ordinary.
I don't want to be the river-girl or the king.
I want to stop turning my longing into folklore
and just say it plain, once, before I lose the nerve—

I made up a hundred legends
so I wouldn't have to tell you the true one:
that I think of you more than I mean to,
that no invented god has ever ached
the way I ache,
plainly,
now,
still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an unrhymed, iambic pentameter poem about the process of writing a song meant to suppress fantasy, incorporating references to the sea and Cuban mythology.
counterfactuals.output:
**Against the Current**

I sit before the page the way a sailor
kneels before tides that took his younger brother,
and ask for words that will not let me dream.
The güije watches from the river's dark,
his green hands folded, waiting for my ink
to loosen like a net and let him through.
I will not let him. I have work to do.

This song must be a wall against the water,
a door of salt no fantasy can open.
Yemayá hums beneath the floorboards, humming
the low blue songs that mothers use to drown
their sons in sleep, and I steal one chord only,
then close my ears against the rest of her,
because too much becomes a current pulling
the whole boat toward the reef it cannot see.

Atabey watches too, that moon of stone
who made the sea before the ships were needed,
before a single sailor learned to leave.
I ask her for a rhythm, not a story—
a beat like waves that break but do not carry,
a tide that comes ashore and empties out
its hands, refusing every shell it finds.

The ceiba stands its ground along the shoreline,
its branches full of spirits I won't summon.
I write instead of anchors, iron, weight,
the ballast in the hull that keeps a vessel
from rising when the wind begins to dream
of harbors it has never had to reach.

By morning it is finished: a song of stillness,
a tune built out of everything I muted.
I play it once. The güije does not answer.
The sea, for now, lies flat as unlit paper.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem about self-cure through art—someone writing a song about Cuban legends and the sea to quiet an unhealthy craving, ending with an ironic twist about their own voice.
counterfactuals.output:
**Singing Down the Thirst**

Midnight, and the bottle waits like a saint
in its niche above the sink—amber,
patient, certain of its worshippers.
He turns instead to the guitar,
its wood the color of rum he hasn't poured,
and begins, because his hands
must do something holy or they will do this.

He sings of Yemayá, mother of salt,
who wears seven skirts the color of drowning,
who combs the tide out of her hair each morning
and never once complains of thirst—
she who contains an ocean
and asks nothing back from it.

He sings the fisherman from Cojímar,
the one who fought the marlin for three days
and lost it to the sharks, to the shore,
to the terrible arithmetic of wanting—
how the old man slept that night
and dreamed of lions, not of fish,
because the body forgives itself in sleep
even when the sea will not.

He sings of Ochún at the river's elbow,
gold bangles, honey in her palms,
sweetness that never once curdled into need—
he borrows her river to run through his own throat,
lets it wash the burn where the burn lives,
lets the ceiba tree's old roots
hold the ground his knees keep begging to leave.

By the fourth hour the craving grows quiet
the way a child grows quiet, not cured,
just listening to something larger
than its own small, insistent hunger.
He does not drink. He sings until dawn
comes up the color of watered rum,
soft, forgivable, undemanding.

He believes, for a moment, he has built
a boat out of language and rowed himself
to some far, sober shore.

But three nights later he cannot sleep
without the guitar in his hands,
cannot pass an evening silent,
finds his own voice thickening, insistent,
the exact grain and rasp
of every old borracho he ever fled
singing boleros at 3 a.m. in the bar on Neptuno—

and understands, too late to be anything
but amused by it: he has not been cured.
He has only changed
what he is helpless to stop craving—

traded one amber for another,
and calls the second one art
because it comes out of his mouth
instead of going in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
